rows.s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires, 21 August 2026
rows.m: Published real-time figure
rows.did: An optometrist who founded Brain Power Inc in 1969 to make ultraviolet-blocking tints and dyes for eyeglass lenses, holding more than 100 patents, then compounded the profits into a buy-and-never-sell portfolio; he is the largest individual shareholder of aerospace supplier Heico.
rows.why: He read patents and annual reports as a technologist rather than trading on price, and he almost never sold, so five decades of compounding ran without realising capital gains. Taking control-adjacent positions in small industrial firms meant he owned the compounding instead of renting it.
rows.obst: He was dyslexic, dropped out of high school and served in the Navy before qualifying as an optometrist; Brain Power then had to defend its lens-chemistry patents against optical manufacturers many times its size.
rows.turn: Buying a large stake in Heico in 1989 and backing the Mendelson familys takeover of it, a position he has held and compounded for more than thirty years.

rows.s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires, 21 August 2026
rows.m: Published real-time figure
rows.did: Signed a royalty-bearing Nike deal as a 1984 rookie instead of a flat endorsement fee, generating roughly 2.4 billion dollars of pretax income from Jordan Brand; bought control of the Charlotte Hornets in 2010 for 275 million dollars and sold the majority in 2023 at a 3 billion valuation.
rows.why: His side took a percentage of shoe revenue rather than a signing cheque, so he owned an annuity on a product line instead of a contract. Nike then built an entire sub-brand around one athlete, which is why the cash flow outlived the playing career by three decades.
rows.obst: Nike was a distant third in basketball in 1984 and he wanted Adidas, which passed; the NBA banned the original black-and-red shoe and fined the team per game, and his 1993 retirement after his fathers murder threatened the brand at its peak.
rows.turn: The 1984 Nike contract negotiated by Deloris Jordan and David Falk, with a royalty on every pair sold, which converted fame into equity.

rows.s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires, 21 August 2026
rows.m: Published real-time figure
rows.did: Took over the failing Idaho Falls company Oil of Melaleuca in 1985 and rebuilt it as Melaleuca, a direct-to-consumer maker of more than 450 household cleaners, supplements and personal-care products with roughly 2 billion dollars of annual sales.
rows.why: He scrapped the multi-level model of front-loaded inventory purchases and replaced it with a monthly reorder of consumables at catalogue prices. Revenue then came from household consumption rather than recruiting, which kept regulators away and attrition low while rivals were being shut down.
rows.obst: The predecessor company was under investigation by the FDA and the Idaho attorney general for illegal medical claims when he took it over; he grew up on a dairy farm without indoor plumbing and had to defend the distributor model in court for years.
rows.turn: The 1985 restructuring that banned distributor inventory loading and made monthly product reorders the only source of revenue.

rows.s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires, 21 August 2026
rows.m: Published real-time figure on a stake of about 2 percent of Cloudflare
rows.did: Co-founded Cloudflare in 2009 at Harvard Business School with Matthew Prince and Lee Holloway out of the Project Honey Pot spam research, offering free DDoS protection and CDN service to any website; it listed in 2019 and passed 2.2 billion dollars of revenue in 2025.
rows.why: Giving the service away to millions of small sites built a global network whose traffic telemetry made the paid enterprise product measurably better. The free tier was a sensor array, not a marketing cost, and Akamai had to charge from the first byte and could never match it.
rows.obst: Investors told them freemium security could not work and that hosting unvetted customers was a legal liability; Cloudflare was hit by the 2017 Cloudbleed memory leak that spilled customer data across the web, and by repeated fights over de-platforming.
rows.turn: The September 2010 TechCrunch Disrupt launch, which took the service from a thousand beta sites to a public network and proved the free tier converted.

rows.s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires, 21 August 2026
rows.m: Published real-time figure covering roughly 70,000 bitcoin plus his Gemini stake
rows.did: Put about 11 million dollars of the Facebook settlement into bitcoin in 2012-13, acquiring close to 1 percent of the supply, then co-founded the New York-chartered exchange Gemini with his twin Tyler in 2014 and filed the first US spot bitcoin ETF application in 2013.
rows.why: They bought a fixed-supply asset early and then built the compliance wrapper around it. A New York trust charter let institutions with fiduciary duties custody bitcoin at Gemini at a time when offshore exchanges were unbankable, so regulation became the moat rather than the obstacle.
rows.obst: The SEC rejected their bitcoin ETF in 2017 and again in 2018; Gemini Earn froze about 900 million dollars of customer funds when Genesis failed in November 2022, drawing an SEC suit and a New York attorney-general fraud action settled in 2024.
rows.turn: The 2013 decision to convert the Facebook litigation proceeds into bitcoin rather than a diversified portfolio.

rows.s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires, 21 August 2026
rows.m: Published real-time figure
rows.did: Worked as a stonemason in his fathers Cisco, Texas business, then with brother Dan founded Frac Tech in 2002 to build and operate hydraulic fracturing pumps; they sold it in May 2011 to a Singapore-led consortium for about 3.5 billion dollars pretax.
rows.why: The shale boom created a shortage of pressure-pumping horsepower, not of acreage. The Wilkses could fabricate pump trucks in their own masonry equipment shop, so they added capacity faster and at lower cost than service majors who had to buy iron on the open market.
rows.obst: Neither brother had petroleum engineering training and they began with a bricklaying crew; their later positions in ProPetro and Carbo Ceramics were hit hard in the 2015-16 and 2020 oil crashes after they had rotated back into the sector.
rows.turn: Selling Frac Tech in May 2011 at the top of the pressure-pumping cycle, converting an operating business into cash and 672,000 acres of western land.

rows.s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires, 21 August 2026
rows.m: Published real-time figure; close to 5 percent of Block plus at least 270M USD of realized sales
rows.did: A St Louis glassblower who lost a 2,000 dollar sale because he could not accept an American Express card, he built the Square card reader with Jack Dorsey in 2009; he remains on the Block board and later founded Invisibly and the nonprofit LaunchCode.
rows.why: Acquirers priced small merchants out with monthly minimums, individual underwriting and terminal leases. Square underwrote risk statistically across a pool and gave the hardware away, which made millions of micro-merchants that banks had refused suddenly addressable.
rows.obst: Card network rules and sponsor banks resisted aggregating unvetted sellers under a single merchant account, and processors called the headphone-jack reader a fraud risk; Square then priced its November 2015 IPO at 9 dollars, well below its last private round.
rows.turn: The 2009 dongle prototype itself, which turned one rejected credit-card sale in a glass studio into a payments company.

rows.s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires, 21 August 2026
rows.m: Published real-time figure
rows.did: An orthopaedic spine surgeon who invented and patented more than 950 devices and methods for minimally invasive spinal fusion, then extracted a 1.35 billion dollar settlement and patent purchase from Medtronic in April 2005 after a decade of litigation.
rows.why: He patented the surgical method and the instruments around the whole procedure, not a single implant. Any manufacturer selling interbody fusion hardware therefore had to license the technique, which made the portfolio unavoidable rather than merely competitive.
rows.obst: Medtronic sued him in 2001, claiming his inventions belonged to it under a 1994 licensing agreement; he counter-sued and spent four years in litigation that could have voided the entire portfolio before a Memphis jury found for him in 2004.
rows.turn: The April 2005 Medtronic settlement, which converted a contested patent estate into 1.35 billion dollars of cash in a single transaction.

rows.s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires, 21 August 2026
rows.m: Published real-time figure
rows.did: Founded Circle in 2013 after building Allaire Corp, maker of ColdFusion sold to Macromedia in 2001, and Brightcove; pivoted Circle from a consumer bitcoin wallet to issuing USDC, the second-largest stablecoin, and listed the company on the NYSE in June 2025.
rows.why: USDC earns the interest on the dollar reserves backing it, so the business is a money-market fund with a payments network attached. Registering with every US regulator while rivals stayed offshore made USDC the only stablecoin banks, exchanges and public companies were willing to hold.
rows.obst: Circle sold its Poloniex exchange at a loss, saw its SPAC merger with Concord collapse in December 2022, and in March 2023 USDC broke its dollar peg when 3.3 billion dollars of reserves were frozen inside the failed Silicon Valley Bank.
rows.turn: The June 2025 NYSE listing, which priced above range and repriced the entire stablecoin sector after the 2022 SPAC failure had written the company off.

rows.s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires, 21 August 2026
rows.m: Published real-time figure
rows.did: Drained his 401k and savings to build Calendly in Atlanta in 2013 after three failed startups, shipping a scheduling link that eliminates the back-and-forth of booking a meeting; took a 350 million dollar investment in 2021 at a 3 billion dollar valuation.
rows.why: Calendly spreads through the recipient rather than the buyer: every meeting link is an advert seen by someone outside the paying company. That drives acquisition cost toward zero, which is why a bootstrapped firm outgrew venture-funded rivals for eight years.
rows.obst: Born in Lagos, he moved to the US at 15 after his father was killed in a carjacking; every Atlanta and Silicon Valley investor he pitched declined, so he funded the first build by emptying his retirement account and hiring developers in Ukraine.
rows.turn: Reaching profitability without venture capital by 2016, which meant he still held almost all the equity when the 2021 round finally arrived.

rows.s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires, 21 August 2026
rows.m: Published real-time figure
rows.did: Cut the feet off a pair of control-top pantyhose in 1998, spent 5,000 dollars of savings and wrote her own patent to found Spanx in 2000; sold a majority stake to Blackstone in late 2021 at a 1.2 billion dollar valuation and stayed on as executive chair.
rows.why: Hosiery mills were run entirely by men who had never asked women what they actually wore under clothes. A footless shaping garment needed no new retail category, slotting straight into the hosiery aisle, and word of mouth meant Spanx spent nothing on advertising for years.
rows.obst: Every North Carolina hosiery mill she cold-called refused her until one owners daughters talked him into a sample run; she wrote the patent herself to avoid legal fees and sold fax machines door to door while developing the product.
rows.turn: Oprah Winfrey naming Spanx a Favorite Thing in November 2000, weeks after launch, which cleared the initial run and opened Neiman Marcus and Bloomingdales.

rows.s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires, 21 August 2026
rows.m: Published real-time figure
rows.did: Co-founded Au Bon Pain in 1981, bought the St Louis Bread Company in 1993 and rebuilt it as Panera, sold Panera to JAB Holding for 7.5 billion dollars in 2017, then put about 175 million dollars into Cava and chaired it through a June 2023 IPO.
rows.why: He identified the fast-casual gap before it had a name: customers would pay roughly double a fast-food ticket for food they believed was real. The rare move was reallocating capital away from himself, selling the original chain to fund the smaller, faster-growing one.
rows.obst: Au Bon Pain was over-levered and stalling by the mid-1990s and he had to divest the founding business in 1999 for 73 million dollars, keeping only the small Bread Company and renaming the entire public company after it.
rows.turn: That 1999 divestiture, which left a single-concept growth company that compounded into the 7.5 billion dollar JAB exit eighteen years later.

rows.s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires, 21 August 2026
rows.m: Published real-time figure
rows.did: Co-founded Black Entertainment Television in 1979 with then-husband Robert Johnson on a 15,000 dollar loan and a 500,000 dollar investment from cable magnate John Malone; Viacom bought BET for about 3 billion dollars in 2001 and she built the Salamander hotel group with the proceeds.
rows.why: Cable operators in 1979 had spare channel capacity and no programming aimed at Black audiences, and advertisers had no way to reach them. BET took the slot cheaply, ran music videos supplied free by record labels, and owned a demographic no broadcaster was serving.
rows.obst: She was written out of the BET founding story for years, divorced Robert Johnson in 2002 and had to liquidate her shares; her Virginia horse-country resort met local resistance and took twelve years and a 2008-crisis delay before opening in 2013.
rows.turn: The 2001 Viacom sale and the 2002 divorce settlement, which converted a co-founder role into independent capital she controlled outright.

rows.s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women, June 2025
rows.m: Published list figure
rows.did: Launched her label from a Manhattan kitchen in February 2004 with a Nolita boutique that nearly sold out on opening day, building an accessible-luxury brand of roughly 1.8 billion dollars in sales across more than 370 stores.
rows.why: She sat between contemporary and true luxury when American women wanted a recognisable logo without a European price. The Reva ballet flat with its medallion became a sub-250 dollar entry product that recruited customers cheaply and funded the rest of the collection.
rows.obst: Her ex-husband and co-founder Chris Burch launched the near-identical C Wonder chain in 2011; the two sued each other in 2012 over the brand and his stake, a fight settled only when he sold half his holding to BDT Capital in 2013.
rows.turn: An April 2005 Oprah Winfrey Show segment that crashed the website and drove millions of visits, converting one New York boutique into a national brand.

rows.s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women, June 2025
rows.m: Published list figure on a majority stake in a company valued above 1B USD in a 2024 minority sale
rows.did: Started making jewellery in an Austin spare bedroom in 2002 with 500 dollars after her first business failed, selling from a tea box shop to shop; built the brand to 152 stores and over 500 million dollars of annual revenue and sold a stake to Berkshire Partners in 2016.
rows.why: She priced colour-swappable stones at 50 to 90 dollars, the band between mall costume jewellery and fine jewellery that department stores had abandoned. The in-store Color Bar made customisation a reason to walk into a shop at the exact moment every other accessory brand was closing them.
rows.obst: Her first venture, a hat shop for chemotherapy patients opened in 2000, collapsed in the post-9/11 retail slump; she launched the jewellery line while pregnant, with no outside capital, and later ran the business through a divorce.
rows.turn: The 2010 decision to open her own stores instead of wholesaling through Neiman Marcus and Nordstrom, which captured the retail margin and the customer relationship.

rows.s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women, June 2025
rows.m: Published list figure; TPG valued the company at 3B USD in 2018 and it has been marked far lower since
rows.did: Arrived in Los Angeles from Communist Romania in 1989 with about 500 dollars and no English, worked as a salon aesthetician, opened her own Beverly Hills brow studio in 1997 and turned it into the cosmetics brand Anastasia Beverly Hills.
rows.why: She created a category that did not exist: eyebrows had no dedicated products. Shaping them to a golden-ratio rule produced a service customers had to repeat every few weeks and a product line with no incumbent to displace, later amplified free by Sephora shelves and Instagram tutorials.
rows.obst: She spoke no English on arrival and was refused by salon owners when she asked to specialise in brows; the 2018 TPG deal marked the company at 3 billion dollars and its value has since fallen sharply as brow fashion moved on.
rows.turn: Shaping Oprah Winfreys brows in the late 1990s and the celebrity referral chain that followed, which turned one studio into a wholesale brand.

rows.s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women, June 2025
rows.m: Published list figure; about 410M USD came from the 2016 LOreal sale
rows.did: Founded IT Cosmetics in 2008 from her San Francisco apartment with her husband and their savings, formulating full-coverage complexion products with plastic surgeons for skin conditions like rosacea; sold the company to LOreal in 2016 for 1.2 billion dollars in cash.
rows.why: Beauty marketing sold aspiration through unblemished models. Demonstrating the product live on women with visible rosacea converted on QVC, a channel where the demonstration is the entire sale and where prestige brands had no presence and no willingness to show real skin.
rows.obst: Investors turned her down for three years and told her women would not buy from someone who looked like the customer; she and her husband put their savings and home into inventory, and her first QVC slot was minutes from being cancelled.
rows.turn: That first QVC broadcast in 2010, when Bye Bye Under Eye sold its 6,000 units in ten minutes and QVC made IT a permanent brand.

rows.s: Forbes-cited estimate of his Flexport stake at about 650M USD; Flexport last marked near 3.8B via Shopify's holding
rows.m: Third-party estimate of a 10 to 12 percent founder stake in a private company, no listed market price
rows.did: Founded Flexport in 2013 as a licensed digital freight forwarder after years running an import business, putting ocean and air bookings, customs filings and container tracking on one dashboard; stepped back as CEO in 2022 and returned in September 2023.
rows.why: Freight forwarding is a brokerage business run on phone calls and per-shipment quotes with no visibility for the shipper. Getting the US customs licence first meant Flexport was the regulated forwarder as well as the software vendor, so it captured the freight margin instead of selling tools to incumbents.
rows.obst: Dave Clark, hired from Amazon as CEO in 2022, left within a year; Petersen came back to an overhired company, cut about 20 percent of staff in 2023, and watched the mark fall from 8 billion dollars as pandemic freight rates collapsed.
rows.turn: The 2022 acquisition of Deliverrs fulfilment network from Shopify, which handed Shopify a 17 percent stake and set the valuation everything is now measured against.

rows.s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women, June 2025
rows.m: Published list figure
rows.did: Spent 25 years in New York family court hearing more than 20,000 cases, then launched Judge Judy in 1996 at 53; it ran 25 seasons paying her about 47 million dollars a year before she moved to Judy Justice on Amazon in 2021.
rows.why: She renegotiated every few years holding the only leverage that matters in syndication, which is being the entire show. In 2017 she sold the back catalogue to CBS for roughly 100 million dollars while keeping ownership of the new programme, so library value accrued to her rather than the studio.
rows.obst: CBS shareholders sued over the 2017 library sale, alleging the studio had underpriced her back catalogue to keep her; before that she was a middle-aged family-court judge with no on-camera experience pitching a genre television executives thought was finished.
rows.turn: A 1993 Los Angeles Times profile that led to a 60 Minutes segment, which producers watched and turned into the Judge Judy pilot.

rows.s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women, June 2025 (fourth-richest self-made woman in US music)
rows.m: Published list figure
rows.co: Les Productions Feeling / Caesars Palace residency
rows.did: Signed at 12 to manager Rene Angelil, who mortgaged his house to fund her first Quebec record, learned English in her twenties, and built the modern Las Vegas residency with A New Day at Caesars Palace from 2003 to 2007 and a second run through 2019.
rows.why: Touring pays once per city and burns the performer. A fixed residency inverts that: the audience travels, the casino funds the venue against hotel and gaming revenue, and the artist plays 4,000 seats a night with no freight, no crew moves and no lost days.
rows.obst: Her manager and husband Rene Angelil died in 2016; she was diagnosed with stiff-person syndrome, disclosed in December 2022, which forced cancellation of the Courage world tour and effectively ended live performance.
rows.turn: The 2003 Caesars Palace deal, a purpose-built 4,100-seat theatre that grossed over 600 million dollars and rewrote how Las Vegas books music.

rows.s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women, June 2025
rows.m: Published list figure
rows.did: Co-founded the options market maker PEAK6 in Chicago in 1997 with 1.5 million dollars and her husband Matt Hulsizer, then used the trading profits to buy or build about fifteen companies, the largest being Apex Fintech, the clearing engine behind SoFi, Webull and eToro.
rows.why: Market making throws off cash uncorrelated with the venture cycle, which funded acquisitions when nobody else could raise. Owning the clearing and custody plumbing under consumer brokerages meant PEAK6 collected a toll on the retail trading boom without ever having to win the retail customer.
rows.obst: She was one of very few women on the Chicago options floor in the 1990s; the 2021 SPAC merger that would have valued Apex at 4.7 billion dollars was cancelled when the blank-cheque market collapsed, stranding the exit she had built toward.
rows.turn: Buying Penson Financials clearing business out of its 2012 bankruptcy and rebuilding it as Apex, which turned a proprietary trading firm into market infrastructure.

rows.s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women, June 2025
rows.m: Published list figure
rows.did: Founded ActOne Group in 1978 in a small Beverly Hills office with 900 dollars borrowed from her mother and a rented fax machine, building it into a staffing, screening and workforce-technology firm with about 890 million dollars of revenue across 33 countries.
rows.why: Contract labour is bought by corporate procurement departments carrying supplier-diversity targets they cannot fill at scale. Being a certified minority and woman-owned vendor large enough to staff nationally won master service agreements that mid-size rivals could not even bid on.
rows.obst: She grew up one of eleven children in segregated Tarboro, North Carolina, and was among the first Black students to integrate her high school; banks would not lend to a young Black woman in 1978, so ActOne grew for years purely on retained earnings.
rows.turn: Landing national corporate accounts in the 1980s that demanded coverage in multiple states, which forced her to build a branch network instead of remaining a single Los Angeles agency.

rows.s: Forbes America's Self-Made Women, May 2024
rows.m: Published list figure; she and husband Alon Cohen together own about a quarter of Houzz
rows.did: Co-founded Houzz in her Palo Alto living room in 2009 with her husband Alon Cohen after failing to find ideas for their own remodel, building a photo-driven marketplace linking homeowners to contractors, architects and products.
rows.why: Renovation is a high-ticket, once-a-decade purchase that search engines serve badly because buyers do not know the vocabulary. A tagged photo library let people point at a finished room instead of typing, which converted browsing into qualified leads professionals would pay a subscription to receive.
rows.obst: Israeli immigrants with no US construction network, they were told the remodeling trade was too fragmented and too offline to digitise; Houzz cut about 10 percent of staff in 2020 and again later as its private mark fell from the 4 billion dollar 2017 peak.
rows.turn: The 2014 Sequoia-led round at a 2.3 billion dollar valuation, which paid for expansion into fifteen countries before rivals localised.

rows.s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women, June 2025
rows.m: Published list figure; roughly three-quarters of it is her Skims stake
rows.did: Co-founded the size-inclusive denim label Good American with Khloe Kardashian in 2016, then co-founded Skims with Kim Kardashian in 2019 as founding partner and chief product officer, holding about 8 percent of a shapewear business later valued in the billions.
rows.why: She supplied the operating half of celebrity brands and took founder equity rather than a licensing fee or consulting rate. The celebrity supplied distribution to hundreds of millions of followers at zero cost, collapsing the customer acquisition spend that normally kills direct-to-consumer apparel.
rows.obst: The daughter of a Jamaican-British single mother on an East London council estate, she left school at 16 with no degree and no fashion-industry family; Good American launched into a market that treated extended sizing as a low-margin afterthought.
rows.turn: Structuring the 2019 Skims launch as an equity partnership rather than a paid operating role, which converted her labour into ownership.

rows.s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women, June 2025
rows.m: Published list figure on a stake of just over 7 percent of BlackLine
rows.did: Cashed out her retirement savings at 40 to found BlackLine in 2001, writing software that automates the account reconciliations behind the corporate month-end close; took it public on Nasdaq in 2016 and returned as co-CEO in March 2023.
rows.why: The financial close still ran on spreadsheets emailed between controllers, and Sarbanes-Oxley turned that into a documented audit finding. Selling automation to the controller as a compliance control, not to the CFO as a productivity tool, put BlackLine in the budget line nobody cuts.
rows.obst: She grew up on an Illinois farm without indoor plumbing, was told by venture investors that a woman with pink hair could not sell to Fortune 500 finance departments, and bootstrapped the company for eleven years before accepting outside money in 2013.
rows.turn: The 2013 Silver Lake Sumeru growth investment, which funded a real enterprise salesforce and set up the 2016 Nasdaq listing.

rows.s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women, June 2025
rows.m: Published list figure following the Sazerac acquisition
rows.did: Invented BuzzBallz as a Texas high-school business teacher grading papers by the pool in 2009, canning ready-made cocktails in a shatterproof plastic sphere, and sold the company to Sazerac in April 2024 in a deal worth at least 500 million dollars.
rows.why: US alcohol moves through a three-tier system in which shelf and cold-vault space is the scarce asset. A round, bright, unbreakable container could be sold at pool decks, stadiums and beaches where glass is banned, winning placements the bottled-cocktail incumbents were structurally unable to contest.
rows.obst: She financed it against her house and her teachers pension, took no outside investors, wrote her masters thesis on the business plan, and had to build her own Carrollton distillery and canning line because no co-packer would run a spherical container.
rows.turn: Getting BuzzBallz into convenience-store cold vaults rather than liquor stores, which moved the product into the impulse channel and pushed revenue past 100 million dollars.

rows.s: SEC Schedule 13G/A: 8,245,050 Warby Parker shares (7.2%) as of 30 Jun 2026; WRBY closed $27.44 on 21 Aug 2026
rows.m: Disclosed beneficial share count x market price, less a disclosed July 2026 sale
rows.did: Co-founded Warby Parker at Wharton in 2010 with three classmates, selling prescription eyeglasses online at 95 dollars with five frames shipped free to try at home; direct-listed the company on the NYSE in September 2021.
rows.why: Luxottica owned frame manufacturing, the Ray-Ban and Oakley brands, LensCrafters and the EyeMed insurance plan at once, holding retail prices near 300 dollars. Designing in-house and selling direct captured the entire margin stack that vertical monopoly had been collecting.
rows.obst: Four business-school students with no optical contacts were refused by frame manufacturers unwilling to risk their Luxottica relationships; at launch the site crashed and hit its first-year sales target in three weeks with 20,000 people waitlisted.
rows.turn: A February 2010 GQ piece calling it the Netflix of eyewear before the site was ready, which built the waitlist and proved people would buy frames sight-unseen.

rows.s: Kellogg paid 600M USD for RXBAR in October 2017; the two founders owned the company outright with no venture capital
rows.m: Modeled from the disclosed sale price and the founder split, after tax, plus his founding stake in David Protein
rows.did: Co-founded RXBAR in his parents Chicago basement in 2013 with 10,000 dollars and childhood friend Jared Smith, printed the entire ingredient list in huge type on the wrapper, and sold to Kellogg for 600 million dollars in 2017; launched David Protein in 2024.
rows.why: Protein bars competed on flavour claims while hiding syrups and isolates. Printing three egg whites, six almonds, two dates on the front made the label the entire marketing, a claim no incumbent could copy without publishing what was actually in theirs.
rows.obst: Rahal is dyslexic and had been placed in special education; RXBAR nearly died in its second year selling case by case to CrossFit gyms, and the founders took no outside capital, so a bad quarter meant no payroll.
rows.turn: The 2015 packaging rewrite that moved the ingredient list to the front of the box, after which sales went from roughly 2 million to over 130 million dollars in two years.

rows.s: Yelp market cap 1.27B USD on 21 Aug 2026; Stoppelman is the largest individual holder at roughly 5 percent
rows.m: Residual stake at current market cap plus fourteen years of disclosed 10b5-1 sales since the 2012 IPO
rows.did: Left PayPal after the eBay sale and founded Yelp in 2004 with Russel Simmons, turning an email-your-friends-for-a-recommendation idea into a crowdsourced local review site; took it public on the NYSE in March 2012 and still runs it.
rows.why: Local businesses were invisible online and had no budget for search advertising. Yelp got the review corpus free from users, then sold those same businesses ads against their own listings, a supply of local content that was expensive for anyone else to recreate.
rows.obst: He turned down Googles roughly 550 million dollar offer in December 2009, then watched Google build a rival local product and push Yelp down its results; Yelp spent a decade filing antitrust complaints in Washington and Brussels while its market value shrank.
rows.turn: Rejecting that Google bid and listing alone in 2012, the decision that capped his fortune at a fraction of what the sale would have paid.

rows.s: 2.87M Box shares (2.08%) per 2026 insider filings; BOX closed $32.91 on 21 Aug 2026
rows.m: Current stake of about 95M USD plus a decade of disclosed 10b5-1 sales, net of tax
rows.did: Started Box in 2005 as a University of Southern California business-plan project with childhood friend Dylan Smith, pivoted it from consumer file storage to enterprise content management, and took it public on the NYSE in January 2015.
rows.why: Box arrived while IT still bought on-premise file servers and employees were already emailing themselves attachments. Selling to the end user first and the CIO second got Box inside companies below the procurement radar, then charged for permissions, retention and compliance.
rows.obst: Box filed to go public in March 2014 and then sat for ten months as the market punished a 169 million dollar annual loss on 124 million of revenue; it had to take a rescue round from TPG and Coatue before finally listing in January 2015.
rows.turn: The 2007 decision to abandon consumer freemium storage for enterprise sales, which cost most of the user base but built a business Dropbox could not undercut on price.

rows.s: Stitch Fix market cap 445.6M USD on 21 Aug 2026; Forbes last listed her at 760M in August 2021
rows.m: Residual low-double-digit founder stake at current market cap plus roughly 47M USD of disclosed share sales
rows.did: Founded Stitch Fix in 2011 from her Harvard Business School apartment, mailing five garments at a time picked by human stylists working off a sizing model, and took it public in November 2017 as the youngest woman ever to lead a US IPO.
rows.why: Buying clothes online was a discovery problem, not a logistics one. A styling fee collected before shipping meant revenue arrived ahead of inventory risk, and every kept-or-returned item fed a fit dataset that made the next box cheaper to fill correctly.
rows.obst: Most Silicon Valley investors who had never shopped for womens clothes passed on the round; her co-founder departed in 2012 and later litigated over equity, and the stock has fallen more than 95 percent from its 2021 high, erasing most of her paper fortune.
rows.turn: The November 2017 IPO, priced below range at 15 dollars after a brutal roadshow, which closed up and forced the market to price the model.
